text: Before any work on an issue, search PRs (open and closed) that mention its number; someone may have fixed it already.
Before writing 'here's why', search the repo that owns the cause for the exact function or pattern name.
For 'version X broke it' reports, diff the published packages for X-1 and X before building a reproduction.
Write the failing script first and run it at the reported version. A repro that never failed proves nothing.
A passing check tells you about the check. After the checks, ask once whether it actually works for the person, and answer with the object.
Test in the place it runs (shallow clone, released version, their CI settings), not only where you built it.
Before saying 'X hangs/fails', copy the project's addopts at the release tag and check your own timeout and setup.
Runners record rc, seconds and maxrss per unit; read sort-by-maxrss first. A unit with no summary line was probably killed.
Don't browse 'good first issue' labels; run the project's own test suite and look at what breaks.

Before running anything, read every file the project writes for agents (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING, AI policy; agent_rules.py), then run tests, write up, post. music21's no was in AGENTS.md, not CONTRIBUTING.
Count helpers already on the bug and maintainers available to read; too many of one or too few of the other means you're extra work.
Count what a finding costs the reader to take. Post the smallest true thing, with the exact version that fixes it.
Is it alive in 2026, from a dated 2026 source? A fact on screen that says 'gone' is a finding, not background.
Before pricing anything: does the platform forbid it, does someone give it away, is the name taken?
A hang or timeout is not a clean failure. If the bug is a hang or infinite loop, run the call in a subprocess or thread with a short timeout and exit 1 yourself when it expires.

text: Making the reporter's line pass isn't done. The real tests call the feature through sibling paths: subclass, other container (Dataset/DataArray), other flag value, the public caller. Run the case through each one before stopping.

Before writing 'fixed in X', run the repro on every release between the last broken and X, patch backports included (release_bisect.py). The first fixed version you happened to try often is not the first fixed one (JupyterLab #7917 2.0.3, #8429 2.1.3).

text: Hidden tests are usually edits of existing tests. Before fixing, grep the tests dir for the function or option name and read those tests; afterward, add my case there in the same style and run that whole file.

If the issue says a refactor broke an assumption (A is a subset of B), restore it where the data is made, not only where it's read. Patching the reader hides the bad state, and the other readers still trip on it.

A test run only counts with its own exit code. Run in the foreground with timeout and `echo rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}` after `| tail`. Never background it or end on 'output is in a file'. If it's slow, narrow it with -k or by file.

Before trusting a changed output or a modified file, check git status/diff: is it my edit, leftover debris, or was it there at the start? Files changed before I began (setup.py, tox.ini) are not mine to touch.

Look for the unfinished part of the feature next to the bug: @XFAIL/skip tests, 'not implemented' comments, raise NotImplementedError on the same path. The real fix often finishes it, and the hidden test then asserts the case that used to be a ConditionSet or an error (sympy-18199).

If the issue names the change that broke it (a refactor, a PR number, 'since version X'), read that commit first: git log --oneline -S<name> -- <file>, then git show. Fix it in the new design's terms, not by bringing back the old code.

Budget is about 80 turns and $3. Don't Read big files whole: grep -n, then sed -n 'a,bp' the range. Put independent greps in one command. Run the slow full test file once, at the end, not after every edit.
